Imagina que quieres decidir si un correo: Imagine you want to decide whether an email is junk. The old way is to write rules by hand: if it contains “offer”, it is junk. La idea de elegir los parámetros que min: The idea of choosing the parameters that minimise the sum of squared errors is from the early nineteenth century: Adrien-Marie Legendre published it in 1805 and Carl Friedrich Gauss claimed to have used it since 1795, which set off a rather ugly priority dispute. The term machine learning was coined by Arthur Samuel in 1959, in an IBM Journal paper about a program that played draughts and improved by playing against itself. Between the one and the other lie a century and a half, and the underlying mathematics barely changed: what changed was the amount of data and the speed of the machines.

La otra forma es no escribir ninguna reg: The other way is to write no rules at all. You write a formula with gaps —some numbers whose values we do not yet know—, you get hold of already classified examples, and you look for the numbers that make the formula get those examples right. Those numbers are the parameters, and finding them is all that “training” means.

It reads: “L of m, n is one over N, times the sum from i equals one to N of m times x sub i plus n, minus y sub i, squared”.

The bracket is a data point's error: what the model says minus what it should say. It is squared for two reasons: so that errors above and below do not cancel, and so that missing by a lot weighs far more than missing by a little.

And the important thing: $L$ is a function of the parameters, not of the data. The data are fixed; what moves is $m$ and $n$. That is why you can differentiate with respect to them and apply everything you already know about optimisation.

They read: “partial derivative of L with respect to m” and “with respect to n”.

They come from differentiating the square with the chain rule: the derivative of $(\ldots)^2$ is $2(\ldots)$ times the derivative of what is inside, which with respect to $m$ is $x_i$ and with respect to $n$ is $1$.

Notice what they say: each data point pushes the parameters in proportion to how much was missed on it. The data points the model gets right push nothing at all, because their error is zero.
